<!------------------ SECTION 1 ------------------> 
# Introduction and general notation

Exposure rating is a tool for insurance pricing that allocates premium to bands
of damage ratios or severity of losses. First ideas were published in @salzmann1963. It is often used to price non-proportional
reinsurance contracts, such as excess of loss (XL) reinsurance. 

Exposure rating uses the loss experience of a similar portfolio of policies to estimate the expected losses of the portfolio to be covered. The method is frequently used as a benchmark when there is no sufficient credible claims history from the client.

In this vignette, we first present the general notation and concepts of loss modelling.
Secondly, we focus on destruction models implemented in the \pkg{mbbefd} package. 
One popular model uses the MBBEFD distribution introduced by @bernegger97.
Finally, we provide an example of pricing of XL contract.



## Loss Distribution

First, let us assume we have perfect information, i.e. we know the loss distribution for a certain risk.

To keep it simple, we assume the loss distribution is log-normal with
a mean ($M$) of 65 and a coefficient of variation ($CV$) of 30%. 
The corresponding log-normal parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ can be derived 
$$
\sigma^2=\log(1+CV^2),~~
\mu =\log(M) - \sigma^2/2 .
$$

The following chart shows the corresponding probability density curve 
$f(x)$, cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ and survival function $S(x)=1-F(x)$. 

```{r cdfsurv, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="PDF, CDF and SF of a lognormal distribution"}
n <- 100
Loss <- seq(1, 150, length = n)
sigma <- sqrt(log(1 + 0.3^2))
mu <- log(65) - sigma^2 / 2
CDF <- plnorm(Loss, mu, sigma)
Density <- dlnorm(Loss, mu, sigma)
Survival <- 1 - CDF
dat <- data.frame(Loss = rep(Loss, 3),
                  Value = c(Density, CDF, Survival),
                  Type = gl(3, n,
                         labels = c("PDF: f(x)",
                                  "CDF: F(x)",
                                  "SF: S(x)=1-F(x)"),
                         ordered = TRUE))
xyplot(Value ~ Loss | Type, data = dat, ylab = "",
       layout = c(3, 1), as.table = TRUE, type = "l",
       par.settings = my.settings,
       par.strip.text = list(col = "white", font = 2),
       scales = list(relation = "free", alternating = 1))
```



In the insurance context, the survival function is  
often called *exceedance probability function*, as it describes the 
probability of exceeding a certain loss.

## Expected Loss

Let's define $X$ as the random variable that describes the ground up loss.
The expected loss 
(in plain English the probability weighted sum of the losses) 
of a positive random variable is then
$$
E[X] =  \int_{0}^\infty x\, f(x) dx.
$$



## Limited Expected Loss

Let's further assume that losses are limited by $\alpha$ in the contract. Then
the limited expected value (LEV), written as $E[X \wedge \alpha]$, is given as
$$
E[X \wedge \alpha] = \int_0^\alpha x \, f(x) dx + \int_\alpha^\infty \alpha \, f(x) dx.
$$

To evaluate this sum of integrals we recall that $F(x)=\int f(x) dx$ and $F(\infty)=1$. Hence
$$
\int_\alpha^\infty \alpha \, f(x) dx = \alpha \int_\alpha^\infty f(x) dx = \alpha - \alpha F(\alpha).
$$

The integration by parts theorem helps with the first part of the integral
$$
\int_0^\alpha x \, f(x) dx = \alpha F(\alpha) - \int_0^\alpha F(x) dx.
$$

Therefore, we retrieve the well-known identity
$$
E[X \wedge \alpha] = \alpha - \int_0^\alpha F(x) dx = \int_0^\alpha 1-F(x) dx
 = \int_0^\alpha S(x) dx.
$$

The integral describes the area above the CDF up to $\alpha$, 
or the area under the survival function up to $\alpha$. In the example
below the limit $\alpha$ was set to 100.


```{r LEV, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=5, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="limited expected value"}
alpha <- 100
fxy <- function(x, y, ...) {
  x1 <- as.numeric(x[x <= alpha])
  if (panel.number() < 2) {
    panel.polygon(c(x1, rev(x1)),
                  rev(c(rep(1, length(x1)), rev(y[x <= alpha]))),
                  col = "skyblue", border = NA)
  } else {
    panel.polygon(c(x1, rev(x1)),
                  c(rep(0, length(x1)), rev(y[x <= alpha])),
                  col = "skyblue", border = NA)
  }
  panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)
}
xyplot(Value ~ Loss | Type,
       data = subset(dat, !Type %in% "PDF: f(x)"),
       ylab = "",
       panel = fxy,
       layout = c(2, 1), as.table = TRUE, type = "l",
       par.settings = my.settings,
       par.strip.text = list(col = "white", font = 2),
       scales = list(relation = "free", alternating = 1))
```

## Loss Cost of a Layer 

Suppose we want to insure the layer of claims between 80 and 100.


```{r LEV2, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=5, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Loss Cost of a Layer"}
alpha1 <- 80
alpha2 <- 100
xyplot(Value ~ Loss | Type,
       data = subset(dat, !Type %in% "PDF: f(x)"),
       ylab = "",
       panel = function(x, y, ...) {
         x1 <- c(x[x >= alpha1 & x <= alpha2])
         if (panel.number() < 2) {
           panel.polygon(
             c(x1, rev(x1)),
             rev(c(rep(1, length(x[x >= alpha1 & x <= alpha2])),
                   rev(y[x >= alpha1 & x <= alpha2]))),
             col = "skyblue", border = NA)
         } else {
           panel.polygon(
             c(x1, rev(x1)),
             c(rep(0, length(x[x >= alpha1 & x <= alpha2])),
               rev(y[x >= alpha1 & x <= alpha2])),
             col = "skyblue", border = NA)
         }
         panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)
       },
       layout = c(2, 1), as.table = TRUE, t = "l",
       par.settings = my.settings,
       par.strip.text = list(col = "white", font = 2),
       scales = list(relation = "free", alternating = 1))
```


The expected loss cost would be the difference between the 
limited expected values of $E[X \wedge 100] - E[X \wedge 80]$
and can be evaluated numerically

```{r checkEL}
sigma <- sqrt(log(1 + 0.3^2))
mu <- log(65) - sigma^2 / 2
S <- function(x) { 1 - plnorm(x, mu, sigma) }
(lyr <- integrate(S, 80, 100)$value)
```

## Increased Limit Factor

On the other hand the ratio of the original loss cost with a limit of 100
to a limit of 80 is called an increased limit factor (ILF):

```{r ILF}
(ILF <- integrate(S, 0, 100)$value / integrate(S, 0, 80)$value)
```

Therefore we would expect the LEV to increase by
`r round(100*(ILF-1), 1)`$\%$ as the limit increases from 80 to 100.

Note ILFs are often used for pricing casualty business.

## Exposure curves

From the loss distribution we could read off the expected loss for any
layer. However, often we will not have that level of information about
the risk. 

Instead, we will have to infer information from others risks that
share similar loss characteristics as a function of the overall exposure, 
assuming that the relative loss size distribution is independent of the 
individual risk characteristic.  

Hence, we will require a view on the expected full value loss cost for the overall
exposure. 

### Normalising loss experience using TIV and MPL

To make risks more comparable we look at ratio of losses to the 
underlying exposure, where the exposure is given as the 
sum insured (SI), or better the total insured value (TIV), 
or perhaps as the maximum probable loss (MPL). 

Other definitions and measures are also popular, such as possible maximum 
loss (PML), estimate maximum loss (EML), or maximum foreseeable loss (MFL).

While the TIV and SI are straightforward to understand, the other metrics can 
be little more challenging to assess. 

Suppose we insure a big production plant with of several buildings against fire. 
It is unlikely that a fire will destroy the whole facility, instead it is 
believed that the distance between the building will ensure that fires can be 
contained in a local area. Hence the MPL might be only the highest value of any 
of those buildings. 

Shifting the metric from loss amounts to damage ratio or destruction rates (loss 
as a % of the exposure metric) allows us to compare and benchmarks risks.



### Analysing deductibles

Most insurance policies are written with a deductible, so that the
insured retains each loss up to the deductible.

Thus, the reinsurer needs to understand, by how much the claims burden is reduced 
for a given deductible. 

From the previous section we have learned how to calculate the limited expected 
value, which is the loss cost to the insured.

The exposure curve (or also called *first loss curve* or *original loss curve*)
is defined as the proportion of the LEV for a given deductible $d$ compared to 
the overall expected claims cost $E[X]$
$$
G(d) = \frac{E[X \wedge d]}{E[X]}.
$$

For our example, using a log-normal distribution and a MPL of 200 we get

```{r ExposureCurve, dev.args=list(pointsize=8), fig.height=3, fig.width=3, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Exposure curve"}
MPL <- 200
ExpectedLoss <- 65
Deductible <- seq(0, MPL, 1)
G <- sapply(Deductible, function(x) {
  LEVx <- integrate(S, 0, x)$value
  LEVx / ExpectedLoss
})
plot(Deductible / MPL, G,
     t = "l", bty = "n", lwd = 1.5,
     main = "Exposure Curve",
     xlab = "Deductible as % of MPL",
     ylab = "% of expected loss paid by insured",
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2)
```

The steepness of the curve is related to the severity of the loss 
distribution. The closer the curve is to the diagonal the greater
the proportion of large loss.

If all losses were total losses then the exposure curve would be 
identical with the diagonal.

Different perils and exposures will have different exposure curves. 
Well known exposure curves are those used by Swiss Re and Lloyd's
(see Section \ref{sec:swissre}).

<!------------------ SECTION 2 ------------------> 
# Destruction rate models

## Classic distributions

From now on, $X$ denotes the destruction rate (or damage ratio), that is the loss
divided by the exposure metric (TIV, SI or MPL), so that $X$ takes values in $I=[0,1]$:
$X=1$ is a total loss.
As already mentioned, the exposure curve function of $X$ is defined as the ratio of the limited expected value and the expectation.
Since $X$ is a positive random variable bounded by 1, $E[X\wedge d]=\int_0^d (1-F_X(x))dx$
and $E[X]=E[X\wedge 1]$, so the exposure curve is
$$
G_X(d) = \frac{\int_0^d (1-F_X(x))dx }{\int_0^1 (1-F_X(x))dx }, \quad d\in I.
$$
$G_X$ is increasing and concave on $I$, with $G_X(0)=0$ and $G_X(1)=1$, see e.g. [@antal03].
Its derivative at 0 gives the mean: $G_X'(0) = 1/E[X]$.

There is a direct link between the distribution function and the exposure curve.
Since $G_X'(x) = (1-F_X(x))/E[X]$ for $x\in[0,1[$,
$$
F_X(x) = \left(1- \frac{G_X'(x)}{G_X'(0)}\right)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x),
$$
defining the exposure curve or the distribution function is equivalent.
In particular, the probability of a total loss is $P(X=1)=G_X'(1^-)/G_X'(0)$.

### Uniform distribution
\label{sec:unif}

The most trivial example of exposure curve is obtained for the uniform distribution on $I$.
We consider $F_X(x)=x$ leading to
$$
G_X(d) 
= d(2-d).
$$


### Beta distribution
\label{sec:beta}

A more interesting example is obtained for the Beta distribution on $I$
(e.g. [@kotzjohnsonbalak94v2])
for which the density is $f_X(x) = x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/\beta(a,b)$ for $x\in ]0,1[$ and $a,b>0$
where $\beta(.,.)$ denotes the
beta function, see e.g. [@nist10].
The distribution function is obtained in terms of the incomplete beta ratio function
$F_X(x) = \beta(x;a,b)/\beta(a,b) = I(x;a,b)$, where $\beta(x;a,b)=\int_0^x t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt$
denotes the incomplete beta function.
Since $E[X]=a/(a+b)$ and $E[X\wedge d] = \frac{a}{a+b} I(d;a+1,b) + d(1-I(d;a,b))$,
and using $I(d;a+1,b) = I(d;a,b) - \frac{d^a(1-d)^b}{a\beta(a,b)}$ (see (8.17.20) in [@nist10]),
we get
$$
G_X(d) = I(d;a,b) - \frac{d^a(1-d)^b}{a\beta(a,b)} + d(1-I(d;a,b)) \frac{a+b}{a}.
$$



## One-inflated distributions
\label{sec:oidistr:generic}


### Characterizations
\label{sec:oidistr:generic:charac}
Let us consider a continuous distribution function $F_0$ of a random variable $X_0$. 
The corresponding distribution function of the one-inflated random variable $X_1$ is 
$$
F_1(x) = (1-p_1) F_0(x) + p_1 \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x).
$$
There is no density but an improper density $(1-p_1)F_0'(x)$ and a probability mass $p_1$ at $x=1$.
Denoting by $G_0$ and $E_0$ the exposure curve and the mean of $X_0$,
$E[X_1\wedge d] = (1-p_1)E_0G_0(d) + p_1 d$ and $E[X_1]=(1-p_1)E_0+p_1$, so that
$$
G_1(d) = \frac{(1-p_1)E_0 G_0(d) + p_1 d}{(1-p_1)E_0+p_1}.
$$



### The one-inflated beta distribution
We consider the one-inflated beta distribution.
Using Section \ref{sec:beta}, we obtain the following distribution function
$$
F_X(x) = 
\systL
0 & \text{if } x<0 \\
I(x;a,b)(1-p_1) & \text{if } 0\leq x <1 \\
1 & \text{if } x\geq 1
\systR
$$
where $I(x;a,b)$ denotes the incomplete beta ratio function.
This leads to a non-null probability at $x=1$, $P(X=1)=p_1$.
The improper density function is 
$$
\tilde f_X(x) = (1-p_1) \frac{x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}}{\beta(a,b)}.
$$
The expectation is
$$
E(X) 
= p_1 + (1-p_1)\frac{a}{a+b}.
$$
The exposure curve is 
$$
G_X(d) =
\frac{(1-p_1) \left(\frac{a}{a+b} I(d;a,b) - \frac{d^a(1-d)^b}{(a+b)\beta(a,b)} + d(1-I(d;a,b)) \right) + p_1d
}{p_1 + (1-p_1)\frac{a}{a+b}}.
$$


## The MBBEFD distribution, first parametrization

We denote this first parametrization by $\mbox{MBBEFD}(a,b)$.
We define the parameter domain $\calD_{a,b}$ as 
\begin{equation}
\calD_{a,b} = \{(a,b)\in\R^2, a+1>0, a(1-b)\geq 0, b>0\}
\cup \{(a,b)\in\R^2, a<-1, 0<b<1\}
\cup \{(a,b), a=+\infty, 0<b<1\}.
\label{eq:paramdomain:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}
Let us note that this domain includes two particular sets $\calD_{a,1}=\{(a,1), a+1>0\}$ and $\calD_{0,b}=\{(0,b), b>0\}$,
for which $a(1-b)=0$.
The set $\{a<-1, 0<b<1\}$ is part of the parameter space
of @bernegger97: it corresponds to $b<1$ and $gb>1$ in the second parametrization
(see Section \ref{sec:mbbefd2p}), where the density is decreasing on $[0,1[$.
The formulas below are the same for $a(1-b)>0$ and for $a<-1$, $0<b<1$,
because the factors $a$, $a+1$, $a+b^x$ and $\ln(b)$ change sign consistently.


### Characterization by the exposure curve
The MBBEFD distribution is defined by the following exposure curve for $(a,b)\in\calD_{a,b}$
\begin{equation}
\forall x\in I,~
G_X(x) = 
\systL
\frac{\ln(\frac{a+b^x}{a+1})}{\ln(\frac{a+b}{a+1})} & \text{if } a(1-b) >0 \text{ or } a<-1 \\
\frac{1-b^x}{1-b} & \text{if } a=+\infty \text{ and } b<1 \\
x & \text{if } a=0 \text{ or } b=1. \\
\systR
\label{expcurve:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}
The two special cases of $a(1-b)=0$ 
correspond to $\calD_{a,1}$ and $\calD_{0,b}$.
Note that the denominator is a normalizing constant to ensure the term belongs to $[0,1]$.



### Distribution, density and quantile functions
Differentiating $G_X$, we obtain the following distribution function
 for $(a,b)\in\calD_{a,b}$
\begin{equation}
\forall x\in I,~
F_X(x) = 
\systL
\left(1-\frac{(a+1)b^x}{a+b^x}\right)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{if } a(1-b) >0 \text{ or } a<-1 \\
(1-b^x)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{if } a=+\infty \text{ and } b<1 \\
\ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{if } a=0 \text{ or } b=1. \\
\systR
\label{cdf:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}
Note that the MBBEFD distribution is a mixed-type distribution with mass probability at $x=1$
\begin{equation}
P(X=1)  = \frac{(a+1)b}{a+b} = p_{a,b},
\label{mass0:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}
which equals to 1 when $a(1-b)=0$. In other words, for $\calD_{a,1}$ and $\calD_{0,b}$, $X$ has a Dirac distribution at $x=1$.
When $a=+\infty$, the total loss probability is $P(X=1)=b$.

The improper density function is
\begin{equation}
\tilde f_X(x) =
\systL
-\frac{a(a+1)b^x\ln(b)}{(a+b^x)^2}\ind_{[0,1[}(x) & \text{if } a(1-b) >0 \text{ or } a<-1 \\
-\ln(b)b^x\ind_{[0,1[}(x)  & \text{if } a=+\infty \text{ and } b<1 \\
0 & \text{if } a=0 \text{ or } b=1. \\
\systR
\label{impd:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}
The quantile function is 
\begin{equation}
\forall p\in [0,1],~
q_X(p) = 
\systL
\frac{\ln\left(\frac{(1-p)a}{a+p}\right)}{\ln(b)} \ind_{[0,1-p_{a,b}[}(p) + \ind_{[1-p_{a,b},1]}(p)  & \text{if } a(1-b) >0 \text{ or } a<-1 \\
\frac{\ln(1-p)}{\ln(b)}\ind_{[0,1-b[}(p) + \ind_{[1-b,1]}(p)   & \text{if } a=+\infty \text{ and } b<1 \\
\ind_{]0,1]}(p) & \text{if } a=0 \text{ or } b=1. \\
\systR
\label{q:mbbefd:ab}
\end{equation}


### Moments
Using the definition of the exposure curve, we have
$E(X) = 1/G_X'(0).$
The expectation for $\mbox{MBBEFD}(a,b)$ is
$$
E(X)=\frac{\ln(\frac{a+b}{a+1})}{\ln(b)} (a+1).
$$
When $a=0$ or $b=1$, the expectation is simply $E(X)=1$.


## The MBBEFD distribution, second parametrization

\label{sec:mbbefd2p}


### Parameter domain

For fitting purposes and for verifying parameter constraints, 
@bernegger97 proposed a second parametrization $\mbox{MBBEFD}(g,b)$.
Using the following parameter $g=1/p_{a,b}$, it is possible to reformulate the $\mbox{MBBEFD}(a,b)$.
That is
$$
g= \frac{a+b}{(a+1)b}
\Leftrightarrow
a=\frac{(g-1)b}{1-gb}.
$$
So $g\geq 1$ guarantees that the total loss probability $P(X=1)=\frac{(a+1)b}{a+b}=1/g$ belongs to $]0,1]$, in addition to $b>0$.
The special case $g=1$ leading to a Dirac distribution at $x=1$ corresponds to $a(1-b)=0$ in the previous parametrization.
The parameter domain is
$$
\widetilde{\calD}_{g,b}= \left\{
(g,b)\in\R^2, b>0, g\geq 1
\right\}.
$$
This domain is simpler than $\calD_{a,b}$, which makes the second parametrization
convenient for fitting.
For $g>1$, it splits into three regions, separated by the special cases $b=1$ and $gb=1$
[see also @gattiwuthrich24, Section 3.1]:

* $D_1=\{b>1\}$, which corresponds to $-1<a<0$;
* $D_2=\{b<1, gb<1\}$, which corresponds to $a>0$;
* $D_3=\{b<1, gb>1\}$, which corresponds to $a<-1$.

The improper density below is decreasing on $[0,1[$ in $D_1$ and $D_3$.
In $D_2$, it is increasing on $[0,1[$ when $g(1+b)\leq 2$, decreasing when $b(2g-1)\geq 1$,
and unimodal otherwise (the sign of its derivative is the sign of $1-gb-(g-1)b^{1-x}$).
On the boundaries, $b=1$ and $gb=1$ give the one-parameter subfamilies
(sometimes called "$g$ only" and "$b$ only") whose formulas are listed below:
they are the limits of the general formulas, so that the distribution is continuous in $(g,b)$.


### Characterization by the exposure curve

The exposure curve is defined for $x\in[0,1]$ as
\begin{equation}
G_X(x)=
\systL
\frac{\ln(\frac{(g-1)b}{1-b}+\frac{1-gb}{1-b}b^x)}{\ln(gb)} & \text{ if } g>1, b\neq 1, b\neq 1/g \\
\frac{\ln(1+(g-1)x)}{\ln( g)} & \text{ if } g>1, b= 1 \\
\frac{1-b^x}{1-b} & \text{ if } g>1, bg= 1 \\
x & \text{ if } g=1 \text{ or } b= 0
\systR
\label{expcurve:mbbefd:gb}
\end{equation}
Note that the case $g>1, bg=1$ implies $g=1/b, b<1$.


### Distribution, density and quantile functions

The resulting distribution function is
\begin{equation}
F_X(x)=
\systL
\left(1- \frac{1-b}{(g-1)b^{1-x}+1-gb}\right)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{ if } g>1, b\neq 1, b\neq 1/g \\
\left(1- \frac{1}{1+(g-1)x}\right)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{ if } g>1, b= 1 \\
(1-b^x)\ind_{[0,1[}(x) + \ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{ if } g>1, bg= 1 \\
\ind_{[1,+\infty[}(x) & \text{ if } g=1 \text{ or } b= 0
\systR
\label{cdf:mbbefd:gb}
\end{equation}
As in the previous parametrization, there is a non-null probability at $x=1$, 
\begin{equation}
P(X=1)  = 1/g.
\label{mass0:mbbefd:gb}
\end{equation}
The improper density function is for $x\in ]0,1[$
\begin{equation}
\tilde f_X(x) = 
\systL
 -\frac{(1-b)(g-1)\ln(b)b^{1-x}}{((g-1)b^{1-x}+1-gb)^2}  & \text{ if } g>1, b\neq 1, b\neq 1/g \\
\frac{g-1}{(1+(g-1)x)^2} & \text{ if } g>1, b= 1 \\
-\ln(b) b^x  & \text{ if } g>1, bg= 1 \\
0 & \text{ if } g=1 \text{ or } b= 0
\systR
\label{impd:mbbefd:gb}
\end{equation}
The quantile function is 
\begin{equation}
\forall p\in [0,1],~
q_X(p) = 
\systL
\left(1-\frac{\ln\left(\frac{gb-1}{g-1} +\frac{1-b}{(1-p)(g-1)}\right)}{\ln(b)}  \right)
\ind_{[0,1-1/g[}(p) + \ind_{[1-1/g,1]}(p) & \text{ if } g>1, b\neq 1, b\neq 1/g \\
\frac{p}{(1-p)(g-1)}\ind_{[0,1-1/g[}(p) + \ind_{[1-1/g,1]}(p)  & \text{ if } g>1, b= 1 \\
\frac{\ln(1-p)}{\ln(b)}\ind_{[0,1-1/g[}(p) + \ind_{[1-1/g,1]}(p) & \text{ if }  g>1, bg= 1 \\
\ind_{]0,1]}(p) & \text{ if } g=1 \text{ or } b= 0
\systR
\label{q:mbbefd:gb}
\end{equation}


### Moments

The first moment follows from the exposure curve.
$$
E(X) = 1/G_X'(0) = 
\systL
\frac{\ln(gb)(1-b)}{\ln(b)(1-gb)} & \text{ if } g>1, b\neq 1, b\neq 1/g \\
\frac{\ln(g)}{g-1}  & \text{ if } g>1, b= 1 \\
\frac{b-1}{\ln(b)} & \text{ if }  g>1, bg= 1 \\
1 & \text{ if } g=1 \text{ or } b= 0
\systR
$$
For $g>1$, the mean is decreasing in $b$, from 1 when $b\to 0$ to $1/g$ when $b\to+\infty$
(the mean is then the total loss probability, as $X$ is concentrated on 0 and 1).
Higher moments have no simple closed form; since $X\in[0,1]$, they are computed numerically
by `mMBBEFD()` as
$$
E(X^k) = \int_0^1 P(X^k>y)dy = \int_0^1 \left(1-F_X(y^{1/k})\right)dy.
$$

## The Swiss Re exposure curves
\label{sec:swissre}

@bernegger97 (Section 4.3) showed that the Swiss Re exposure curves $Y_1$ to $Y_4$,
used in property per risk exposure rating, and the Lloyd's curve for industrial risks
are very well approximated by $\mbox{MBBEFD}(g,b)$ curves whose parameters lie on a
curve indexed by a single parameter $c$:
$$
b(c) = e^{3.1-0.15c(1+c)}, \quad g(c) = e^{c(0.78+0.12c)},
$$
with $c=1.5, 2, 3, 4$ for $Y_1$ to $Y_4$ and $c=5$ for the Lloyd's curve.
The larger $c$, the smaller the total loss probability $1/g$ and the more concave
the exposure curve (small losses are more frequent).
The function `swissRe()` returns $b(c)$ and $g(c)$; note that $b$ comes first,
so the parameters should be selected by name.

```{r swissre}
swissRe(c(1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

```{r swissreplot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3, fig.width=3, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Swiss Re exposure curves"}
par(cex = 0.8, mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
d <- seq(0, 1, length = 201)
cc <- c(1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5)
plot(d, d, type = "l", lty = 2, xlab = "Deductible as % of MPL",
     ylab = "% of expected loss paid by insured", bty = "n")
for (i in seq_along(cc))
{
  p <- swissRe(cc[i])
  lines(d, ecMBBEFD(d, g = p["g"], b = p["b"]), col = i)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste0("c=", cc), col = seq_along(cc), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

# Fitting methods and pricing examples

## Fitting methods: MLE and TLMME

We consider two fitting methods, namely the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
and the total-loss-moment matching estimation. Both methods are 
implemented in the `fitDR` function of the \pkg{mbbefd} package.


As its name suggest, the maximum likelihood function consists in maximizing 
the likelihood function defined as
$$
\calL(\theta, x_1,\dots,x_n)= \prod_{i=1}^n f_X(x_i),
$$
where $f_X$ denotes the density of the loss random variable $X$ and
$\theta$ is the parameter vector.
When $X$ is a continuous non-inflated distribution, $f_X$ is the usual
density function (obtained by differentiating the distribution function).
When $X$ is a mixed-type distribution with a non-null probability $P(X=1)$,
$f_X(x)$ is $F_X'(x)$ for $x\neq 1$ and $P(X=1)$ for $x=1$, i.e. the density
with respect to the sum of the Lebesgue measure and the Dirac mass at 1
[see e.g. @coxwermuth98].

For example when considering the beta distribution, the likelihood function to be maximized is
$$
\calL((a,b), x_1,\dots,x_n)= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{x_i^{a-1}(1-x_i)^{b-1}}{\beta(a,b)}.
$$
For the MBBEFD distribution, with $n_1$ the number of total losses, the log-likelihood is
$$
\log\calL((g,b), x_1,\dots,x_n) = -n_1\log(g) + \sum_{i: x_i<1} \log \tilde f_X(x_i),
$$
where $\tilde f_X$ is the improper density of Section \ref{sec:mbbefd2p}.
Since $g$ drives both the total loss probability and the shape of $\tilde f_X$,
the estimate exists even if there is no total loss in the data ($n_1=0$), but $1/g$
is then identified only through the shape of the distribution below 1:
`fitDR()` raises a warning in that case, as total losses may have been removed or capped.

For one-inflated distributions, the likelihood factorizes: the maximum likelihood estimator of $p_1$
is the proportion of total losses $n_1/n$, and the parameters of $F_0$ are estimated
on the observations below 1 only.

For the MBBEFD distribution, `fitDR()` maximizes the log-likelihood with the analytical
gradient in four steps:

1. starting values are obtained by an unconstrained fit on transformed parameters;
2. the log-likelihood is maximized separately on the three regions $D_1$, $D_2$ and $D_3$
of Section \ref{sec:mbbefd2p}, under inequality constraints (the constraints differ between
regions, notably in the first parametrization);
3. each of these fits is refined by an unconstrained maximization in $(\log(g-1), \log(b))$,
which covers the whole parameter space: the log-likelihood is continuous across
the boundaries $b=1$ and $gb=1$, which constrained optimizers cannot reach;
4. the fit with the highest log-likelihood is retained.

Standard errors are obtained from the observed information matrix, i.e. the inverse of the
Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the estimate.

The total-loss-moment matching estimation consists in matching the
total loss and the first moments of a distribution.
That is we solve the system
$$
\systL
P(X = 1;\theta) = tl_n \\
E(X; \theta) = \bar x_n\\
\vdots \\
E(X^k; \theta) = m_{n,k}\\
\systR
\text{ where }
\systL
tl_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ind_{x_i =1},\\
\bar x_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\\
m_{n,k} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i)^k.
\systR
$$
The number of equation $k+1$ equals the number of parameters.
This method is relevant only for distributions with a probability mass at 1
(one-inflated and MBBEFD distributions), as for classic
continuous distributions such as the beta distribution we know that $P(X=1)=0$.

For the MBBEFD distribution, the system has an explicit solution [@bernegger97, Section 4.1]:
the first equation gives $g=1/tl_n$, and since the mean is decreasing in $b$ from 1 to $1/g$
(Section \ref{sec:mbbefd2p}), the second equation has a unique root $b$ if and only if
$0 < tl_n < \bar x_n < 1$. It is computed by a one-dimensional root search.
When this condition does not hold, `fitDR()` returns `NA` with a warning.

The \pkg{fitDR} function of the \pkg{mbbefd} package returns an object of class
\pkg{"fitDR"} inheriting from the \pkg{"fitdist"} class for which generic functions
are available \pkg{print, plot, summary, gofstat}.
There is also a bootstrap procedure implemented in the \pkg{bootDR} function.

## Examples

Let us fit some distributions with a simulated dataset based on a mixture
of two distributions (regular beta and mbbefd).

```{r simufit, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(123456)
x <- c(rbeta(50, 3, 1 / 2), rmbbefd(50, 1 / 2, 1 / 10))
f1 <- fitDR(x, "mbbefd", method = "mle")
summary(f1)
b1 <- bootDR(f1, niter = 25)
summary(b1)
```

```{r denplot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=4, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Histogram, fitted density"}
par(cex.main = 0.8,  cex.lab = 0.8, cex.axis = 0.8, cex = 0.8)
denscomp(f1, demp = TRUE, main = "Histogram and fitted density", xlegend = "topright")
```

```{r bootstrapplot,echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=6, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Bootstrap heatmap and scatter plot"}
par(cex.main = 0.8,  cex.lab = 0.8, cex.axis = 0.8, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
plot(b1, enhance = TRUE, main = "Bootstrapped value of parameters")
```


The estimated total loss probability $1/g = (a+1)b/(a+b)$ is
`r round(tlmbbefd(f1$estimate["a"], f1$estimate["b"]), 3)`, to be compared with the
empirical proportion of total losses `r etl(x)`: the maximum likelihood estimator does not
match the total losses exactly, because both parameters also determine the continuous part.
The bootstrap summary reports the number of bootstrap samples for which the optimization
converged.

The graphs correspond respectively to the histogram (and empirical density)
against the fitted density and a two-dimensional level curve and scatter plot
for bootstrap parameters.

As in the \pkg{fitdistrplus} package, we can compare multiple fits on the
same graph or with the same statistics. We just have to pass a list of
\pkg{"fitDR"} objects.

```{r simufit1}
f2 <- fitDR(x, "oibeta", method = "mle")
gofstat(list(f1, f2))
```

The Anderson-Darling statistic is infinite for both fits: its computational formula
involves $\log(1-F(x_i))$, which is infinite at the total losses since $F(1)=1$, so this
statistic is not suited to data with total losses. The information criteria favour the one-inflated beta
distribution on this mixture.



```{r simufit2, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=7, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="comparison on cdf and pdf plots"}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex.main = 0.8,  cex.lab = 0.8, cex.axis = 0.8, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
cdfcomp(list(f1, f2), leg = c("mbbefd", "oibeta"))
denscomp(list(f1, f2), leg = c("mbbefd", "oibeta"),
         ylim = c(0, 4), xleg = "topleft")
```

Of course, we can also compare the different fitted exposure curves
using the function \pkg{eccomp}. That is

```{r simufit3, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=4, warning=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Comparison on exposure curves"}
par(cex = 0.8)
eccomp(list(f1, f2), leg = c("mbbefd", "oibeta"), do.points = FALSE)
```



## Computation of premium rate (example)

### Exposure rating of a risk profile

Let us consider a risk with MPL $M$ and premium $P$, with an expected loss ratio $ELR$, 
and a layer $L$ xs $D$. If the destruction rate $X$ of the risk has exposure curve $G_X$, 
the expected loss of the layer is
$$
ELR \cdot P \cdot \left( G_X\left(\min\left(\frac{D+L}{M},1\right)\right) - G_X\left(\min\left(\frac{D}{M},1\right)\right) \right),
$$
since $E[\min(\max(MX-D,0),L)] = M\left(E[X\wedge \frac{D+L}{M}] - E[X\wedge \frac{D}{M}]\right)$.
In practice, the cedant provides a risk profile, i.e. risks grouped in MPL bands 
with their premium, and the formula is applied to each band with its mean MPL [@ExposureRating2004].

### The Swiss Re example

The following example is taken from the Swiss Re technical publication [@ExposureRating2004].
It is the aim to find the risk premium for a per risk WXL cover 
(fire only) with the limits
$$
\mbox{CHF } 3,500,000 \mbox{ xs CHF } 1,500,000.
$$
The cover protects the retention of a proportional (surplus) treaty with a maximum 
retention of CHF 5,000,000 MPL: for larger risks, the cedant keeps only this amount 
and the same proportion of the premium.

The gross net premium income (GNPI) is CHF $95,975,000$ in 2004, 
with an expected loss ratio of 55%. Therefore we have a view on the 
mean expected loss cost.

The risk profile given by the cedant is from the year 2002.
However, instead of re-indexing the historical data to 2004, we back-index
the layer to 2002 with a factor of $457/550=0.83$ (construction cost index):
$$
\mbox{CHF } 2,908,182
\mbox{ xs CHF } 1,246,364,
$$
and the maximum retention becomes CHF 4,154,545, which is also the exhaustion 
point of the layer.
 
The data presented below is from the client, with pre-selected
exposure curves: the Swiss Re curves $Y_1$ to $Y_4$, approximated by the MBBEFD 
curves with parameter $c$ of Section \ref{sec:swissre}.
The policies have been grouped into different exposure bands. 
The mean MPL is simply the average of the lower and upper band.
Amounts are in CHF thousands.

```{r SwissReExample, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Client <- scan(textConnection(paste(
  "150 75 250 200 400 325 600 500 800 700 1000 900 1250 1125 1500 1375 1750 1625",
  "2000 1875 2500 2250 3000 2750 4000 3500 5500 4750 9000 7250 12500 10750 18000 15250",
  "24000 21000 36000 30000 48000 42000 72000 60000 90000 81000")), quiet = TRUE)
MaxMPL <- Client[seq(from = 1, to = length(Client), by = 2)]
MeanMPLGrossLoss <- Client[seq(from = 2, to = length(Client), by = 2)]
GrossPremium <- scan(textConnection(
  "33434 14568 6324 4584 3341 1405 1169 683 613 554 700 552 1194 1490 4177 3527 3249 2712 2588 1988 657 1918"
), quiet = TRUE)
ExposureCurve <- c(rep(1.5, 3), rep(2.0, 3), rep(3.0, 4), rep(4.0, 12))
ClientData <- data.frame(MaxMPL, MeanMPLGrossLoss,
                         GrossPremium, ExposureCurve)
ClientData2 <- ClientData
names(ClientData2) <- c("Max MPL", "Mean MPL",
                        "Gross Premium", "Exposure Curve Parameter c")
library(pander)
panderOptions("big.mark", ",")
panderOptions("table.split.cells", 8)
pander(ClientData2, justify = rep("right", ncol(ClientData2)))
```

The premium of each band is computed in three steps:

1. the net MPL is the mean MPL capped at the retention, and the net premium is the 
gross premium multiplied by net MPL / mean MPL;
2. the deductible is expressed as a proportion $d$ of the net MPL, capped at 100%;
3. the share of the losses in the layer is $1-G_X(d)$, since the layer covers the 
net MPL above the deductible, and the XL premium is the net premium times this share.

```{r SwissRe2}
#exposure curve of the Swiss Re curve with parameter c
ecSwissRe <- function(d, c)
{
  p <- swissRe(c)
  ecMBBEFD(d, g = p["g"], b = p["b"])
}
#XL premium by band
XLPremiumByBand <- function(Deductible, Retention, MeanMPL, GrossPremium, C)
{
  NetMPL <- pmin(MeanMPL, Retention)
  NetPremium <- GrossPremium * NetMPL / MeanMPL
  DedPerMPL <- pmin(Deductible / NetMPL, 1)
  XLShare <- 1 - mapply(ecSwissRe, DedPerMPL, C)
  data.frame(NetMPL, NetPremium, DedPerMPL, XLShare, XLPremium = NetPremium * XLShare)
}
D <- 1500 * 457 / 550 #deductible
R <- 5000 * 457 / 550 #retention = exhaustion point of the layer
bands <- XLPremiumByBand(Deductible = D, Retention = R,
                         MeanMPL = ClientData$MeanMPLGrossLoss,
                         GrossPremium = ClientData$GrossPremium,
                         C = ClientData$ExposureCurve)
```

```{r SwissRe3, echo=FALSE}
bands2 <- cbind(ClientData[, c("MaxMPL", "MeanMPLGrossLoss")],
                round(bands$NetMPL), round(bands$NetPremium),
                round(100 * bands$DedPerMPL, 1), round(100 * bands$XLShare, 1),
                round(bands$XLPremium, 1))
names(bands2) <- c("Max MPL", "Mean MPL", "Net MPL", "Net Premium",
                   "Deductible % of MPL", "XL share %", "XL premium")
pander(bands2, justify = rep("right", ncol(bands2)))
i1 <- which(ClientData$MaxMPL == 4000)
i2 <- which(ClientData$MaxMPL == 90000)
```

Let us detail three types of bands.

* **Bands below the deductible.** When the mean MPL is below the deductible, 
the losses never reach the layer: $d=100\%$, $G_X(d)=1$ and no reinsurance premium 
is needed.
* **Bands between the deductible and the retention.** For the band with a maximum MPL 
of CHF 4m, a mean MPL of CHF 3.5m and a gross premium of CHF 1,194k, the deductible is 
$1{,}246/3{,}500=`r round(100*bands$DedPerMPL[i1], 1)`\%$ of the MPL. 
From the exposure curve with $c=4$, the cedant keeps $G_X(d)=`r round(100*(1-bands$XLShare[i1]), 1)`\%$ 
of the expected losses, so the share of the layer is `r round(100*bands$XLShare[i1], 1)`$\%$ 
and the reinsurance premium for this band is CHF 1,194k $\cdot$ 
`r round(100*bands$XLShare[i1], 1)`$\% =$ `r round(bands$XLPremium[i1], 1)`k.
* **Bands above the retention.** For the band with a maximum MPL of CHF 90m and a mean MPL 
of CHF 81m, the cedant keeps CHF 4,155k of each risk, so the net premium is 
CHF 4,155k/81,000k $\cdot$ 1,918k $=$ `r round(bands$NetPremium[i2], 1)`k.
The deductible is $1{,}246/4{,}155=`r round(100*bands$DedPerMPL[i2], 1)`\%$ of the net MPL, 
the cedant keeps $G_X(d)=`r round(100*(1-bands$XLShare[i2]), 1)`\%$ of the losses, and the reinsurance 
premium is `r round(bands$NetPremium[i2], 1)`k $\cdot$ `r round(100*bands$XLShare[i2], 1)`$\% =$ 
`r round(bands$XLPremium[i2], 1)`k.

### Premium Rate

For the overall portfolio, the risk premium rate is the sum of the XL premiums 
multiplied by the expected loss ratio of 55%, divided by the net premium volume:

```{r SwissRe4}
ULR <- 0.55
(pr <- ULR * sum(bands$XLPremium) / sum(bands$NetPremium))
#risk premium for 2004 and rate on line
(riskprem <- pr * 95975000)
riskprem / 3.5e6
```

We get a premium rate of `r round(100*pr, 2)`$\%$ of the net premium volume 
(CHF `r format(round(sum(bands$NetPremium)), big.mark=",")`k in 2002), that is a risk premium of 
CHF `r format(round(riskprem), big.mark=",")` for 2004 and a rate on line of `r round(100*riskprem/3.5e6, 1)`$\%$.
@ExposureRating2004 obtains $1.636\%$, CHF 1,570,151 and $44.9\%$ with the 
tabulated Swiss Re curves: the small differences come from the MBBEFD approximation 
of the curves $Y_1$ to $Y_4$ and from rounding (for instance, the publication reads 
$21\%$ and $25\%$ for the two bands detailed above).
